statement: how do you mourn a parent who was never kind to you when they were alive? feeling crushed and guilty all at once.
passage: Jacob tore his clothes, and put sackcloth on his waist, and mourned for his son many days. All his sons and all his daughters rose up to comfort him, but he refused to be comforted. He said, “For I will go down to Sheol to my son mourning.” His father wept for him.
plain: Jacob tore his clothes and mourned his son for many days. All his children tried to comfort him, but he refused, saying he would grieve until he joined his son in the grave.

statement: I was my mother's carer for a long time and now that she's gone I feel relief, and that makes me feel like a monster.
passage: When I saw the lonely figure of my mother vanish in the distance, a sense of regret settled heavily upon me. I felt suddenly weak, as if I might fall limp to the ground. I was in the hands of strangers whom my mother did not fully trust. I no longer felt free to be myself, or to voice my own feelings. The tears trickled down my cheeks, and I buried my face in the folds of my blanket. Now the first step, parting me from my mother, was taken, and all my belated tears availed nothing.
plain: Watching my mother disappear, I felt heavy regret and sudden weakness. Among strangers she didn't fully trust, I could no longer be myself or speak my feelings, and crying now changed nothing.

statement: My friend is grieving and I want to be there for her, but I keep worrying that I'll say something wrong. Should I keep checking in or give her space?
passage: When you see anyone weeping for grief, either that his son has gone abroad or that he has suffered in his affairs, take care not to be overcome by the apparent evil, but discriminate and be ready to say, “What hurts this man is not this occurrence itself—for another man might not be hurt by it—but the view he chooses to take of it.” As far as conversation goes, however, do not disdain to accommodate yourself to him and, if need be, to groan with him. Take heed, however, not to groan inwardly, too.
plain: When you see someone weeping over a loss, do not be overcome; what hurts him is not the event but the view he takes of it. Talk with him kindly, even groan with him, but do not groan inwardly.

statement: He is a genuinely decent guy on paper, provides and doesn't yell, but I feel completely lonely sitting right next to him on the sofa. Is companionship supposed to feel this empty?
passage: I find it wholesome to be alone the greater part of the time. To be in company, even with the best, is soon wearisome and dissipating. I love to be alone. I never found the companion that was so companionable as solitude. We are for the most part more lonely when we go abroad among men than when we stay in our chambers. A man thinking or working is always alone, let him be where he will. Solitude is not measured by the miles of space that intervene between a man and his fellows.
plain: Being alone most of the time is good for me; even the best company soon tires me. No companion is as good as solitude. We are often lonelier among people than alone; solitude is not measured in miles.

statement: We broke up months ago and I still check every one of his accounts daily. He treated me badly, I know that, but I can't make myself block him because part of me is still waiting.
passage: Thinking: ‘They did wrong to me, but what can I possibly do?’ you get rid of resentment.
plain: When someone has wronged you, you can let go of resentment by thinking: what can I possibly do?

statement: My parents adore my little sister and I get blamed for everything. If I'm upset I'm "attention seeking". If I bring it up they scream at me.
passage: Everything has two handles: one by which it may be borne, another by which it cannot. If your brother acts unjustly, do not lay hold on the affair by the handle of his injustice, for by that it cannot be borne, but rather by the opposite—that he is your brother, that he was brought up with you; and thus you will lay hold on it as it is to be borne.
plain: Everything has two handles: one you can carry it by and one you cannot. If your brother wrongs you, don't take hold of his wrong; take hold of the fact that he is your brother, raised with you.

statement: We're moving abroad for my wife's sake and our kids' future and my family is acting like I'm stealing their grandchildren. My sister called me selfish. How do I do this without losing them completely?
passage: Beg our Lord to grant you perfect love for your neighbour, and leave the rest to Him. He will give you more than you know how to desire if you constrain yourselves and strive with all your power to gain it, forcing your will as far as possible to comply in all things with your sisters' wishes although you may sometimes forfeit your own rights by so doing. Forget your self-interests for theirs, however much nature may rebel; when opportunity occurs take some burden upon yourself to ease your neighbour of it.
plain: Ask God for perfect love of your neighbour and leave the rest to Him. Push yourself to give way to others' wishes, put their interests before yours however much you resist, and take burdens off them.

statement: I'm the eldest in an immigrant family and every time I mention moving out my mother asks what will happen to her. I feel like I owe them everything. how to become independent without this guilt :/
passage: Your most radiant garment is of the other person’s weaving; Your most savory meal is that which you eat at the other person’s table; Your most comfortable bed is in the other person’s house. Now tell me, how can you separate yourself from the other person?
plain: Your finest clothes are woven by others, your tastiest meal is at another's table, your most comfortable bed is in another's house; so how can you separate yourself from other people?
work: Sand and Foam: A Book of Aphorisms

statement: My girlfriend woke me up crying because her school friends went out without her again. It keeps happening. I don't know how to help her or what to say.
passage: You have taken my friends from me. You have made me an abomination to them. I am confined, and I can’t escape. My eyes are dim from grief. I have called on you daily, Yahweh. I have spread out my hands to you.
plain: You have taken my friends away and made them turn from me. I'm shut in with no escape, and my eyes are dim with grief. Every day I call to you, God, reaching out my hands.

statement: My manager calls out my mistakes in front of the whole office but is lovely to everyone else. When her name pops up on Teams my heart races. Push through or leave?
passage: When you know that what you say behind someone’s back is untrue, false, and pointless, then to the best of your ability you should not speak. When you know that what you say behind someone’s back is true and correct, but pointless, then you should train yourself not to speak. When you know that what you say behind someone’s back is true, correct, and beneficial, then you should know the right time to speak. When you know that your sharp words in someone’s presence are untrue, false, and pointless, then to the best of your ability you should not speak. When you know that your sharp words in someone’s presence are true and correct, but pointless, then you should train yourself not to speak. When you know that your sharp words in someone’s presence are true, correct, and beneficial, then you should know the right time to speak.
plain: If what you'd say about someone, behind their back or sharply to their face, is false, don't say it. If true but useless, train yourself not to say it. If true and helpful, know the right time to say it.

statement: I know I need to leave but the thought of having no job terrifies me. This job pays for my family's life. How do people actually do this?
passage: But if you keep turning round and looking about, in order to see how much you may carry away with you, and how much money you may keep to equip yourself for the life of leisure, you will never find a way out. No man can swim ashore and take his baggage with him.
plain: If you keep looking back to see how much wealth you can take with you into a quieter life, you will never get out. No one can swim to shore carrying their luggage.

statement: checked my bank balance after groceries and cried in the car. doing everything 'right' and still sinking further into debt every single month.
passage: What tears and toil does money wring from us! Greed is wretched in that which it craves and wretched in that which it wins! Think besides of the daily worry which afflicts every possessor in proportion to the measure of his gain! The possession of riches means even greater agony of spirit than the acquisition of riches. And how we sorrow over our losses—losses which fall heavily upon us, and yet seem still more heavy! And finally, though Fortune may leave our property intact, whatever we cannot gain in addition, is sheer loss!
plain: Money costs us tears and toil. Greed is miserable both in craving and in getting; owning wealth brings more anguish than gaining it, losses hurt more than they should, and whatever we fail to add feels like loss.

statement: Diagnosed again. He laughs it off but I'm so scared and sad and I don't know if I can do this a second time.
passage: Be not afraid. Think not how many times you fail. Never mind. Time is infinite. Go forward: assert yourself again and again, and light must come.
plain: Do not be afraid, and do not count how many times you fail, for time is endless. Keep going, assert yourself again and again, and light will come.

statement: I cheated. She forgave me, I haven't done it again, and I still can't forgive myself. I don't feel like I deserve to feel alive again.
passage: I often entertained the impulse of ending my life then and there; but the thought of my kind old father kept me back. For I reflected, not how bravely I had the power to die, but how little power he had to bear bravely the loss of me. And so I commanded myself to live. For sometimes it is an act of bravery even to live.
plain: During a long illness I was often tempted to end my life, but thinking of my kind old father held me back: he could not bear to lose me. So I ordered myself to live. Sometimes even living takes courage.

statement: Someone I trusted crossed a boundary, and I keep wondering whether I somehow encouraged it. I know that sounds irrational, but I can't stop going over the situation in my head.
passage: Yes, my own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, who ate bread with me, has lifted up his heel against me.
plain: Even my close friend, someone I trusted and shared meals with, has turned against me.

statement: company asking me to relocate abroad with family. i absolutely love this job but dont want to compromise family at all. please guide is it right choice for long run
passage: Now Yahweh said to Abram, “Leave your country, and your relatives, and your father’s house, and go to the land that I will show you.
plain: God told Abram to leave his country, his relatives and his father's home, and go to a land God would show him.

statement: Everyone compliments how composed and capable I am, but on the inside I feel like a clueless child pretending to be an adult. One slip and everyone will see through it.
passage: If you would improve, be content to be thought foolish and dull with regard to externals. Do not desire to be thought to know anything; and though you should appear to others to be somebody, distrust yourself. For be assured, it is not easy at once to keep your will in harmony with nature and to secure externals; but while you are absorbed in the one, you must of necessity neglect the other.
plain: To improve, be willing to be thought foolish about external things, and do not want to seem knowledgeable. If others think you important, distrust yourself; you cannot both keep your will in harmony with nature and secure externals.

statement: I go to Mass, I pray every day, and I haven't felt God in a long time. I've tried everything. What am I doing wrong?
passage: Perhaps some of us here will remember that there are moments in our lives when, tired of all these ratiocinations of dull and dead logic, tired of plodding through books — which after all teach us nothing, become nothing but a sort of intellectual opium-eating — we must have it at stated times or we die — tired with all this, the heart of our hearts sends out a wail: “Is there no one in this universe who can show me the light? If Thou art, show the light unto me. Why dost Thou not speak? Why dost Thou make Thyself so scarce, why send so many Messengers and not Thyself come to me? In this world of fights and factions whom am I to follow and believe? If Thou art the God of every man and woman alike, why comest Thou not to speak to Thy child and see if he is not ready?” Well, to us all come such thoughts in moments of great depression; but such are the temptations surrounding us, that the next moment we forget.
plain: At times, tired of dead logic and useless books, the heart cries to God: if you exist, show me the light, speak to me yourself, tell me whom to follow. Such thoughts come in deep depression, then we forget.

statement: I had a near-death experience in an accident last month and suddenly my corporate goals feel completely meaningless. How do you integrate back into everyday trivialities after that?
passage: How can our principles become dead, unless the impressions [thoughts] which correspond to them are extinguished? But it is in thy power continuously to fan these thoughts into a flame. I can have that opinion about anything, which I ought to have. If I can, why am I disturbed? The things which are external to my mind have no relation at all to my mind.⁠—Let this be the state of thy affects, and thou standest erect. To recover thy life is in thy power. Look at things again as thou didst use to look at them; for in this consists the recovery of thy life.
plain: Your principles die only if the thoughts behind them go out, and you can keep fanning those into flame. Outside things have no hold on your mind. You can recover your life by seeing things again as you once did.

statement: adopt a rescue dog yesterday and he finally rested his head on my knee while sleeping. my heart is so full.
passage: Even those with a dart stuck in the breast, piercing the heart moment by moment, are able to get some sleep. So why not I, whose dart is drawn out? I don’t lie awake tense, nor do I fear to sleep. The days and nights don’t disturb me, as I see no decline for myself in the world. That’s why I lie down full of sympathy for all living creatures.
plain: Even people with a dart in the heart get some sleep, so why not the Buddha, whose dart is drawn out? He lies down unafraid and untroubled, sees no decline for himself, and is full of kindness for all beings.

statement: My girlfriend just broke up with me. It came out of the blue. Even though our relationship hasn't been good for a while, I really didn't think that she was considering breaking up. I'm angry, but I'm also sad, and I'm also questioning how much of it was my fault. At this age, to suddenly not have a partner, I'm really scared about the future.
passage: My days are past, my plans are broken off, as are the thoughts of my heart.
plain: My days are over, my plans broken off, and so are the hopes of my heart.

statement: I was hoping to get into my favorite college of choice, and I've been working on it for so long now. Today I just got a rejection letter. I really worked hard for this. I put all my energies in, and now I don't get to go to the college of my choice. I dreamed of this all my life, and it's so heartbreaking that this is not going to happen for me. I just don't know how I'll ever stop feeling sad about this.
passage: If our young men miscarry in their first enterprises they lose all heart. If the young merchant fails, men say he is ruined. If the finest genius studies at one of our colleges and is not installed in an office within one year afterwards in the cities or suburbs of Boston or New York, it seems to his friends and to himself that he is right in being disheartened and in complaining the rest of his life. A sturdy lad from New Hampshire or Vermont, who in turn tries all the professions, who teams it, farms it, peddles, keeps a school, preaches, edits a newspaper, goes to Congress, buys a township, and so forth, in successive years, and always like a cat falls on his feet, is worth a hundred of these city dolls. He walks abreast with his days and feels no shame in not “studying a profession,” for he does not postpone his life, but lives already. He has not one chance, but a hundred chances.
plain: Young people lose heart at their first failure. But a sturdy youth who tries trade after trade and always lands on his feet is worth a hundred pampered ones. He doesn't postpone life; he has a hundred chances, not one.

statement: My dog died. He's been my friend, my closest friend, for the last 12 years. He's been my support. He's been my reason to come home every day, and now he's gone.
passage: At this grief my heart was utterly darkened; and whatever I beheld was death. My native country was a torment to me, and my father's house a strange unhappiness; and whatever I had shared with him, wanting him, became a distracting torture. Mine eyes sought him every where, but he was not granted them; and I hated all places, for that they had not him; nor could they now tell me, "he is coming," as when he was alive and absent. I became a great riddle to myself, and I asked my soul, why she was so sad, and why she disquieted me sorely: but she knew not what to answer me.
plain: Grief darkened my heart; everything I saw was death. Home tormented me, and all I'd shared with my friend became torture without him. I searched everywhere and hated every place for lacking him. I became a riddle to myself.

statement: I'm so confused about the different choices I have to make. On one hand, I could prioritize my career and make progress there. On the other hand, I could be a better parent and spend more time with my children. Neither of these seems negotiable. If I spend more time with my children, I'll hold a grudge against them because I didn't get to achieve all that I wanted to in my career. If I devote myself to my career, then I feel like I'm a bad parent. It feels like a lose-lose situation.
passage: Some of our children are our justifications and some are but our regrets.
plain: Some of our children justify our lives, and some are only our regrets.
work: Sand and Foam: A Book of Aphorisms

statement:
I got into a huge fight with my mother today. It's the same old thing. She keeps trying to pressure me to live in accordance with how she thinks I should. I just hate it when she does this. It drives me mad. She's been doing this to me all her life. I just don't know how to deal with it anymore.

If I say something, she twists it, turns it around, and makes it into something that's my fault. If I don't say anything, then I just end up feeling shit, like she's mistreating me, and if I distance myself, then I feel guilty. I don't even know if there's a way out of this.
passage: Everything has two handles: one by which it may be borne, another by which it cannot. If your brother acts unjustly, do not lay hold on the affair by the handle of his injustice, for by that it cannot be borne, but rather by the opposite—that he is your brother, that he was brought up with you; and thus you will lay hold on it as it is to be borne.
plain: Everything has two handles: one you can carry it by and one you cannot. If your brother wrongs you, don't take hold of his wrong; take hold of the fact that he is your brother, raised with you.

statement: I'm just so lonely. Everyone else has their person. Everyone seems to have a good community around them, and I'm just so lonely all the time. There's no one that I can really talk to. It's just me alone all the time with my own thoughts. I don't know. I try to reach out to people, but it always ends badly. I don't even want to try to reach out, but again, I feel lonely all the time.
passage: The moment you isolate yourself, everything hurts you. The moment you expand and feel for others, you gain help. The selfish man is the most miserable in the world. The happiest is the man who is not at all selfish.
plain: Cut yourself off and everything hurts you; reach out and feel for others and you are helped. The selfish man is the most miserable; the happiest has no selfishness at all.

statement: I just found out that my best friend is cheating on his wife. I've been getting really close to her the last couple of years, and I deeply care for her. I'm just stuck in this moral dilemma now. I don't know what to do. If I don't say anything to her, I'm letting her continue being cheated on, and that feels really wrong. If I say anything to her, I am betraying my friend. I don't know what to do. It feels like I'm stuck between a rock and a hard place.
passage: Love a friend, and keep faith with him: But if you reveal his secrets, You shall not pursue after him; For as a man has destroyed his enemy, So have you destroyed the friendship of your neighbor. And as a bird which you have loosed out of your hand, So have you let your neighbor go, and you will not catch him again: Pursue him not, for he is gone far away, And has escaped as a gazelle out of the snare. For a wound may be bound up, and after reviling there may be a reconcilement; But he that reveals secrets has lost hope.
plain: Love a friend and keep faith. If you reveal their secrets, don't chase them; the friendship is gone like a bird let loose. A wound can heal and insults be forgiven, but betraying secrets leaves no hope.

statement: My boss sucks. Every single day, he just finds new ways to annoy me. He takes credit for my work. He belittles me at every opportunity that he gets. He keeps me stuck at the level that I am, not allowing me to grow. I can't afford to risk leaving this job, and the market is so bad that I can't seem to find anything half decent. Every day is starting to turn into torture.
passage: When we begin to work earnestly in the world, nature gives us blows right and left and soon enables us to find out our position. No man can long occupy satisfactorily a position for which he is not fit. There is no use in grumbling against nature’s adjustment. He who does the lower work is not therefore a lower man. No man is to be judged by the mere nature of his duties, but all should be judged by the manner and the spirit in which they perform them.
plain: When we start working seriously, life's knocks soon show us where we belong, and no one stays long in a role they don't suit. Lower work doesn't make a lower person; judge people by the spirit in which they work.

statement: I turned 58 yesterday, and since then, I've had a difficult time accepting my age. Where did all the last few years go? It feels like my life is coming to a close, and I may not have achieved even close to what I wanted to.
passage: Let us cease to desire that which we have been desiring. I, at least, am doing this: in my old age I have ceased to desire what I desired when a boy. To this single end my days and my nights are passed; this is my task, this the object of my thoughts,—to put an end to my chronic ills. I am endeavouring to live every day as if it were a complete life. I do not indeed snatch it up as if it were my last; I do regard it, however, as if it might even be my last.
plain: Let us stop wanting what we have long wanted; in old age I no longer desire what I did as a boy. My one task is ending my chronic faults. I live each day as complete, perhaps my last.

statement: Lately, I've been questioning the meaning of life. What's the point of it all? Everyone keeps running towards an unknown goal, but at the end of the day, we're all just going to die. What's the point of everything?
passage: We always forget that this world is a means to an end, and not an end itself. If this were the end we should be immortal here in our physical body; we should never die. But we see people every moment dying around us, and yet, foolishly, we think we shall never die; and from that conviction we come to think that this life is the goal.
plain: We forget this world is a means, not an end. If it were the end, we would never die. We see people dying all around us, yet foolishly think we never will, and so take this life as the goal.

statement: The world is such a dark place sometimes. I don't know how to not let that darkness creep into me. This war, fire, people fighting, cruelty, poverty, ugliness everywhere I turn. It's just so disheartening to see.
passage: As I have said to the Indian people again and again, if there is the darkness of centuries in a room and we go into the room and begin to cry, “Oh, it is dark, it is dark!”, will the darkness go? Bring in the light and the darkness will vanish at once.
plain: If a room has been dark for centuries and we go in crying how dark it is, will the darkness leave? Bring in light and the darkness vanishes at once.

statement:
I finally met someone I think I can spend the rest of my life with. After all these years of relationships that didn't come close to working out, I finally found one that may potentially work, but he wants me to convert to his faith. I'm just not a religious person. I don't really give it much importance.

On one hand, does it really matter? It's important to him, why not? On the other hand, it's kind of like lying, right, if I don't believe in it and am just doing it for the external sake of it. Should he even get to dictate something so important? Why can't he accept me for who I am?
passage: Believe me, the question is not whether we wear the religious habit or not, but whether we practise the virtues and submit our will in all things to the will of God. The object of our life must be to do what He requires of us: let us not ask that our will may be done, but His.
plain: What matters is not whether we wear religious dress but whether we live the virtues and give our will over to God's in everything. Our aim should be to do His will, not ask for ours.

statement: I told my best friend that my ex-boyfriend messaged me and that I decided to message him back just so that we could both have closure. She did the worst thing she could do to me: she told my boyfriend, who is really insecure about my past relationship. She already knows this. She knows how insecure he is and how he gets about this, and she knows why I chose to message him back. Why would she do something like this to me? This has already shaken me to my core.
passage: Yes, my own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, who ate bread with me, has lifted up his heel against me.
plain: Even my close friend, someone I trusted and shared meals with, has turned against me.

statement: I've been going to church since I was a child, and now, at the age of 28, it just all feels so meaningless. Every Sunday, we go sit and listen to sermons, and at the same time, everyone's behaving in ways that are just not compatible with the basic morality. Forget about what religion says. Why do I keep up with this? Why should I keep up with this sham? I should just quit the church.
passage: I cannot afford to be irritable and captious, nor to waste all my time in attacks. If I should go out of church whenever I hear a false sentiment I could never stay there five minutes. But why come out? the street is as false as the church, and when I get to my house, or to my manners, or to my speech, I have not got away from the lie.
plain: I can't spend my time irritably attacking. If I left church at every false sentiment, I'd never stay five minutes. But why leave? The street is just as false, and in my own manners and speech the lie remains.

statement: I'm so ugly, and I don't know what to do about it. Everyone else is so beautiful. I hate looking at myself in the mirror. I hate my body. It just makes me feel so depressed. Every morning, I dread the thought of standing in front of the mirror.
passage: If you would protect your body, guard your mind. If you would renew your body, beautify your mind. Thoughts of malice, envy, disappointment, despondency, rob the body of its health and grace. A sour face does not come by chance; it is made by sour thoughts. Wrinkles that mar are drawn by folly, passion, and pride.
plain: To protect your body, guard your mind; to renew it, beautify your mind. Malice, envy, disappointment and gloom rob the body of health and grace; sour thoughts make a sour face, and folly, passion and pride make wrinkles.

statement: I've been trying to lose weight for pretty much all my life, and yet I've had no success. I've been trying to get over this self-loathing and just be happy with the way I am. Today, someone made a comment that just broke my heart, and I've gone back into the spiral. The only thing I know to do when I feel this way is to run and soothe myself by eating.
passage: You may be frightened to lose a hundred pounds, but there may be others who would not even wink if they lost all the money they had in the world. There have been such men and still there are. Why do you dare to judge them according to your standard?
plain: You may dread losing a hundred pounds, while others would not blink at losing everything they own; such people have existed and still do. Why judge them by your own standard?

statement:
Where do I even start? I was much too hard on my child, bro. When he was growing up, I just wanted him to be strong enough to be able to face this world in all its cruelties. I wanted him to not have to struggle the way I did, so I was trying to prepare him for the world.

I understand now that I hurt him deeply, and I was the source of his suffering rather than protecting him from the world. Now he doesn't even speak to me. I don't know how to fix this, and I can't get over the guilt.
passage: If I put myself in the place of my child, and we stand in one thought and see that things are thus or thus, that perception is law for him and me. We are both there, both act. But if, without carrying him into the thought, I look over into his plot, and, guessing how it is with him, ordain this or that, he will never obey me.
plain: If I put myself in my child's place and we see things together, that shared understanding guides us both. But if I guess at his situation from outside and give orders, he will never obey me.

statement: I told my wife about my promotion at work, and she just said, "Oh, that's nice," and that's it. She didn't say anything else. I could tell that not only did she not care, but it almost looked like she was unhappy that I got something that I was too eagerly looking forward to. I think she grudges me having a good career because she has been stuck in hers for such a long time without any forward momentum.
passage: Has any man been preferred before you at a banquet, or in being saluted, or in being invited to a consultation? If these things are good, you ought to rejoice that he has obtained them; but if bad, be not grieved because you have not obtained them.
plain: If someone is preferred over you at a dinner or in greetings, rejoice for him if these things are good; if they are bad, do not grieve at missing them.

statement: I spent all my life earning money to make up for the fact that I grew up so poor. Now I have all the money that I want, but I'm still so unhappy. That sense of anger and resentment towards my childhood poverty hasn't gone away. All the money in the world does not seem to satiate the anger and hurt that I have inside me. I don't know what to do.
passage: But my wife treats me badly. Well, if any man asks you what this is, say, my wife treats me badly. Is there then nothing more? Nothing. My father gives me nothing. (What is this? my father gives me nothing. Is there nothing else then? Nothing); but to say that this is an evil is something which must be added to it externally, and falsely added. For this reason we must not get rid of poverty, but of the opinion about poverty, and then we shall be happy.
plain: My wife treats me badly, my father gives me nothing: that is all that happened. Calling it evil is a false addition. So rid yourself not of poverty but of your opinion of it, and you will be happy.

statement: I just got engaged after years and years of hoping I'd find someone. I finally did. This is the happiest day of my life.
passage: You smiled and talked to me of nothing and I felt that for this I had been waiting long.
plain: You smiled and talked to me about nothing, and I felt this was what I had long been waiting for.
